extracted.intended_audience: Reviewers of CHI 2025 submissions (CHI program committee members, associate chairs)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for performing peer review of submissions to the CHI 2025 conference, including what criteria to use, expectations about review content and length, and policies on prior publication, replication, transparency, and use of AI tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary criterion — contribution to HCI
rubrics_metrics.description: Your primary criterion for judging a paper is: Does this submission provide a strong contribution to the field of HCI?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize there are many ways a paper can make a contribution to HCI and review the paper appropriately (see 'Contributions to CHI' and 'Guide to a Successful Submission' for types and associated criteria). In all cases, a CHI paper must make an original research contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall recommendation must match written appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers decide the overall recommendation (Accept with minor revisions, Revise and Resubmit, and Reject) on each submission with written appraisal that matches with their recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure your written comments justify and align with the overall recommendation. Inconsistent pairing of recommendation and rationale weakens the decision process at PC meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review quality and sufficient detail
rubrics_metrics.description: A high-quality review is typically about a page of written text; very short reviews are frustrating for authors, tend to be less constructive, and hurt the review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always put yourself in the author’s position: what level of detailed feedback would you like to see? Write a detailed review whether or not you like the paper—short positive or negative reviews without justification will not provide support for decisions, especially in presence of counter-reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer responsibility for accuracy (including references) and use of AI
rubrics_metrics.description: As a reviewer, you are responsible for the content and accuracy of your reviews, including the references cited. This is especially relevant if you choose to use AI tools based on Large Language Models (LLM), which are prone to producing plausible sounding garbage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you use AI tools for editing or drafting portions of your review, verify accuracy and relevance of any output, especially factual claims and citations. Follow the ACM Policy on using AI tools in reviewing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality and handling of manuscript content
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining confidentiality is crucial in the review process; quoting or disclosing papers under review must be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copying and pasting content from a manuscript into an LLM or online tool may compromise confidentiality—reviewers should avoid sharing unpublished content with tools that may store or process the data. It is the reviewer’s responsibility to understand implications of any such tool and abide accordingly. See ACM Policy links provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and prior-publication policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Content appearing at CHI should be new and groundbreaking. Material previously published in widely disseminated archival publications should not be republished unless the work has been significantly revised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A significant revision is roughly characterized as containing more than 25% new content (new insights, new results) and substantially amplifying or clarifying the original material; this is subjective and left to reviewer/committee judgment. Exceptions: translations from other languages (with original author as author/co-author and clearly stated) are permitted; non-archival venues (workshops, posters, Late-Breaking Work) do not count as prior publication. Work independently published after CHI submission (during review period) should not be held against authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication as a valid contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Replicating other researchers’ work is not precluded; constructive replication can be a significant contribution to HCI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitted replications must include sufficient information to allow future replications. Efforts to include complete, well-organized supplementary material (software, analysis code, data) should be rewarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of transparency in the way research results are reported can be a ground to doubt the contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See the 'Transparency' section in the Guide to a Successful Submission for how transparency expectations vary by contribution type (e.g., methods reporting, data/code availability, pre-registration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper length must be commensurate with contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: In CHI 2025, paper length should be commensurate with their contribution. There is no arbitrary maximum (or minimum) length to papers, but clarity and conciseness of writing is considered vital to a high-quality submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must identify whether their paper is short (less than 5,000 words), long (typically 7,000–8,000 words), or excessively long (more than 12,000 words). Reviewers should realize that appropriate content differs by length category: short papers should present brief, focused contributions and reviewers should not ask for more than appropriate; excessively long papers must justify why a shorter contribution is not suitable; papers judged incommensurate with length (too long: repetitive/verbose; too short: omitting important details, neglecting related work, or tampering with formatting) will be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length categories (author declaration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are required to identify if their paper is: short (less than 5,000 words), long (typically 7,000–8,000 words), or excessively long (more than 12,000 words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical, long submissions are expected to be approximately 7,000–8,000 words. Excessively long submissions (beyond 12,000 words) must provide strong justification for why a shorter contribution is not suitable; only in very exceptional cases will such submissions be considered for full review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not penalize for subcommittee fit
rubrics_metrics.description: As a reviewer, you should not judge the paper by how well it fits the subcommittee theme(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many papers will not cleanly fit into a particular subcommittee for a variety of reasons; the subcommittee organization exists to improve reviewer matching. Evaluate submissions on their own quality and contribution; any topic is valid as long as it fits within the interests of a reasonable fraction of the overall CHI audience.
